paper_title: RSIFlow: Adaptive Self-Improvement Workflows with an Evolving Meta-Agent

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in complex tasks, including code generation, tool use, and multi-hop question answering. Existing self-improvement methods enhance agent performance through model optimization, harness evolution, and executable artifact refinement, while recursive self-improvement (RSI) further extends optimization to the improvement mechanisms themselves. However, adapting self-improvement workflows to evolving performance bottlenecks while improving workflow orchestration through execution feedback remains a key challenge. We propose \textbf{RSIFlow}, a \textbf{R}ecursive \textbf{S}elf-\textbf{I}mprovement framework that integrates adaptive work\textbf{flow} orchestration with meta-agent capability evolution. RSIFlow diagnoses performance bottlenecks from task-agent trajectories and environmental feedback to dynamically select component-specific improvement workflows. The meta-agent then distills workflow outcomes into component-specific skills and cross-component principles, evolving its own harness to improve subsequent workflow orchestration. Experiments across six benchmarks and two backbone models show that RSIFlow achieves the SOTA average performance on all benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate the contributions of adaptive workflow orchestration and meta-harness evolution. Code is available at https://github.com/1HUAN1/RSI-Flow.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled agents to tackle complex tasks in coding, tool use, and multi-hop question answering (Yang et al., 2024; Schick et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023). To continuously enhance the development of agents capabilities in task domains, existing methods have adopted complementary approaches, including evolving execution harnesses 1 Figure 1: Motivation of RSIFlow. (A) Two coupled challenges in RSI. (B) The execution loop of RSIFlow. (Zhang et al., 2025), optimizing model parameters (Luo et al., 2025), and refining executable artifacts (Novikov et al., 2025). These routes can be organized into self-improvement workflows that propose and evaluate changes using task feedback. Beyond executing such workflows, recursive selfimprovement (RSI) seeks to strengthen not only task-solving capabilities but also the mechanisms that generate subsequent improvements (Zhang et al., 2026c; Duan et al., 2026). Research on agent self-improvement spans three increasingly broad scopes of optimization. Component-level approaches optimize predefined part of the system, such as the model or the harness (execution workflows) (Luo et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b). System-level approaches coordinate updates across components, including joint modelharness optimization and feedback-driven selection of update targets (Chen et al., 2026d,b; Hebbar et al., 2026). Meta-level approaches make improvement procedures editable through operator scheduling, program modification, and recursive skill evolution (Tan et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026c; Wang et al., 2026). These developments expand both what can be modified and how modifications are organized. However, broader editability alone does not establish how effectively workflow addresses the agents current bottlenecks, or whether the ability to organize that workflow improves with experience. This motivates central question: how can RSI systems adapt self-improvement workflows to evolving bottlenecks while learning to organize these workflows more effectively? We formulate this challenge as dynamic workflow adaptation in RSI, where adapting bottlenecks and evolving workflow orchestration must be considered together. As illustrated in Fig. 1, selfimprovement workflows must adapt to bottlenecks that vary with task requirements and the agents capability state. Even within fixed domain, successful updates can reshape these bottlenecks and alter the effectiveness of subsequent workflow orchestration. Meanwhile, workflow orchestration is itself capability that can improve through experience. Feedback from workflow execution supports the accumulation and refinement of reusable knowledge for diagnosis, workflow selection, and execution. These processes form feedback loop: task-level updates reshape improvement requirements, while workflow experience refines the orchestration capability that guides subsequent updates. To address this challenge, we propose RSIFlow, framework that couples adaptive workflow orchestration with meta-agent capability evolution. We instantiate three self-improvement workflows targeting the Harness, Model, and Artifacts. metaagent uses execution trajectories and environmental feedback to diagnose the task agents bottlenecks, select workflow, and orchestrate candidate generation and validation. It then distills orchestration outcomes into component-specific skills and crosscomponent principles to revise its own harness, including execution procedures and skill invocation. This experience-driven self-revision closes recursive feedback loop in which workflow orchestration outcomes refine the orchestration mechanism that guides subsequent improvements. Our main contributions are: We formulate dynamic workflow adaptation as key challenge in RSI, highlighting the coupling between evolving performance bottlenecks and continual refinement of workflow orchestration. We propose RSIFlow, which adaptively organizes self-improvement workflows and uses their observed outcomes to evolve the metaagents own harness, including its execution procedures and reusable skills. We evaluate RSIFlow across six benchmarks and two backbones, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline in 11 of the 12 benchmark backbone settings. Ablations support the benefits of both adaptive workflow orchestration and meta-harness evolution.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Component-Specific Self-Improvement. Many approaches to agent self-improvement optimize single predefined component. STaR (Zelikman et al., 2022) improves model parameters by repeatedly fine-tuning on self-generated rationales that yield correct answers. AFlow (Zhang et al., 2025) searches code-represented workflows, while Recursive Harness Self-Improvement (Lee et al., 2026) refines prompt-level harness specifications using pairwise feedback over revision histories. Related approaches include DSPy (Khattab et al., 2024) for language-model pipeline optimization, GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2026) for reflective prompt evolution, and ADAS (Hu et al., 2025) for metaagent-guided search over agent programs. In contrast, AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025) evolves candidate programs through execution-based evaluation, targeting task artifacts rather than the agents improvement procedure. Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023) iteratively revises outputs using selffeedback, while Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) retains verbal reflections to guide subsequent attempts and Voyager (Wang et al., 2024) accumulates reusable executable skills. Co-Harness (Chen et al., 2026d) and HarnessForge (Chen et al., 2026b) connect external structure and internal capability by alternating harness refinement with model optimization. Their coupled updates address modelharness compatibility, but the prescribed update order leaves open how to adapt workflow orchestration targets to evolving bottlenecks. Adaptive and Recursive Self-Improvement. Beyond prescribed alternation, SIA (Hebbar et al., 2026) uses trajectory and performance feedback to choose between harness and weight updates, while its selection policy relies on frozen language2 Figure 2: Overview of RSIFlow. (A) Definition of task domains and agent workflows. (B) The Task-Agent executes tasks to collect trajectories and feedback. (C) The Meta-Agent retrieves skills to adaptively orchestrate workflows. (D) Workflow results are distilled into skills, principles and Meta-Harness. The updated Meta-Harness guides subsequent orchestration, closing the recursive self-improvement loop. model prior. HASE (Luo et al., 2026) integrates task solving and harness editing into one action space and trains the policy with GRPO. complementary direction makes the improver itself editable: Hyperagents (Zhang et al., 2026c) coevolves task-agent and meta-agent programs and demonstrates transferable improvement strategies, whereas MetaSkill-Evolve (Wang et al., 2026) recursively updates task skills and their improvement procedures on different timescales. Building on these complementary directions, RSIFlow couples bottleneck-aware workflow orchestration with feedback-driven Meta-Harness evolution.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: recursive coupling We presented RSIFlow, selfadaptive framework improvement workflow orchestration with Meta-Agent evolution. Using accumulated execution feedback, the Meta-Agent identifies Task-Agent bottlenecks and selects Model, Harness, or Artifacts workflows. It distills successful and unsuccessful outcomes into reusable skills and principles to evolve its Meta-Harness. Across six benchmarks and two backbones, RSIFlow outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline in 11 of 12 settings. Ablations validate both mechanisms, while budget analyses show favorable performancebudget trade-off. These results demonstrate that continual MetaAgent evolution enhances system effectiveness alongside adaptive workflow orchestration.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: RSIFlow is primarily evaluated using Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B as Task-Agent backbones. This setting is particularly relevant to resource-constrained agent deployments, where adaptive workflow orchestration enables targeted modifications to identified bottleneck components, while Meta-Agent evolution further improves bottleneck diagnosis and orchestration capabilities. However, whether these benefits remain significant with larger backbone models and at cluster scale remains unexplored. Future work will extend the evaluation to largerscale settings to assess the scalability of RSIFlow. RSIFlow couples the Task-Agent and MetaAgent, evolving the Meta-Harness through reusable skills and general principles to improve workflow orchestration without updating the Meta-Agents model parameters. However, this process introduces additional computational overhead, while adopting lower-cost Meta-Agent may compromise evolution gains. Moreover, the stability of experience-driven Meta-Harness updates remains to be fully investigated. Future work will explore counterfactual analysis to identify Meta-Agent deficiencies, apply targeted local modifications, and investigate Meta-Agent parameter optimization to improve evolution efficiency and stability.

sections.title: A Experimental Setup
sections.content: We evaluate self-improvement across code generation, tool use, and multi-hop question answering. This section describes the six benchmarks, the update mechanisms of the baselines, and the experimental configurations. Appendix gives the algorithms for the three intervention routes. A.1 Training and Reporting Data Our evolution pool contains 3,000 distinct training tasks, partitioned into five task-disjoint batches of 600 tasks each. Each round uses 200 codegeneration tasks, 200 tool-use tasks, and 200 multihop questions. The fixed reporting set contains 744 tasks. Table 4 gives the dataset-level allocation. Code generation. TACO (Li et al., 2023) contains algorithmic programming problems that require implementing program from naturallanguage specification and satisfying its input/output contract. We use 1,000 training problems from the TACO portion of the DeepCoderPreview-Dataset . The selected tasks include standard-input/output and function-based interfaces, with correctness assessed by executing the submitted program against task-specific tests. They provide execution trajectories and feedback for improving program construction, interface handling, and algorithmic reasoning. The allocation contributes 200 tasks per evolution round; HumanEval+ and MBPP+ are reserved for reporting evaluation. Tool use. EnvScaler (Song et al., 2026) provides executable, stateful environments in which agents solve tasks through sequences of tool calls. Each task specifies user goal and an initial environment state; the agent must choose tools, construct arguments, and adapt its actions to returned observations. Task-specific validation checks assess whether the resulting state satisfies the goal. We allocate 1,000 scenarios to training, comprising 824 from the source datasets train split and 176 from its heldout split. Both source partitions are assigned to the training role in our study; tool-use reporting uses BFCL-v3 and ACEBench. Each evolution round contains 200 EnvScaler scenarios. Different training tasks may share an environment, so the round-disjoint allocation refers to task instances rather than environment families. Multi-hop answering. HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018) contains questions that question require combining evidence across Wikipedia passages, including bridge and comparison questions. 2WikiMultiHopQA (Ho et al., 2020) requires following multi-hop relations across entities and combining the retrieved facts into an answer. We select 500 questions from the official training split of each dataset. The Task-Agent retrieves evidence through the search interface and produces an answer, providing trajectories for improving evidence retrieval and multi-step reasoning. Each round uses 100 HotpotQA and 100 2WikiMultiHopQA training questions. Reporting uses separate fixed set of 100 questions from each datasets official development split. Allocation and data roles. Code, tool use, and multi-hop QA each account for one third of the training pool, giving domain ratio of 1:1:1. Within QA, HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA have equal weight. The five training batches are fixed with split seed 42 and contain distinct task IDs. These counts describe the task allocation; candidate retries and reuse of eligible training trajectories do not create additional distinct tasks. Training and reporting use the separate source partitions described above, with overlap checks and feedback isolation specified in Appendix A.3. A.2 Benchmark Descriptions The reporting set contains 744 tasks: 342 codegeneration tasks, 202 tool-use tasks, and 200 multihop questions. Each method is evaluated on the same task IDs with the same benchmark-specific scorer. Table 5 summarizes the task counts and reported metrics. Code generation. HumanEval+ asks the agent to implement Python function from its signature and natural-language specification. Its 164 tasks test functional correctness, including edge cases exposed by the augmented EvalPlus tests (Liu et al., 2023). MBPP+ asks for short Python programs from natural-language descriptions and illustrative tests, covering basic algorithms, data structures, and program construction. We use frozen 178task subset of MBPP+ v0.2.0. For both benchmarks, task succeeds when the final submitted program passes the base and augmented test suites. We report system pass@1: one final submission per task after the allowed agent execution. HumanEval+ uses v0.1.10, and both benchmarks use EvalPlus revision 26d6d00 with the recorded parser and process-isolation adapters. 12 Table 4: Distribution of training and reporting tasks. Training counts denote distinct tasks; the per-round column describes each of the five evolution batches. dash indicates that dataset is not used in that role. Domain Dataset Code Tool use SearchQA Total TACO (DeepCoder subset) HumanEval+ MBPP+ Code subtotal EnvScaler BFCL-v3 ACEBench Tool-use subtotal HotpotQA 2WikiMultiHopQA SearchQA subtotal Training total Training per round Reporting total 1,000 1,000 1,000 1,000 500 500 1,000 3, 200 200 200 200 100 100 200 600 164 178 342 152 50 100 100 200 744 Counts refer to task instances rather than generated trajectories. Tool use. BFCL-v3 evaluates function selection and argument construction in single-call, multiplecall, parallel-call, relevance, and multi-turn settings (Patil et al., 2025). These settings cover complementary aspects of tool use: selecting an appropriate function, supplying the required arguments, coordinating multiple calls, and determining whether an available tool is relevant to the request. The multi-turn tasks also test whether the agent maintains context across stateful tool interactions, connecting individual call decisions to the evolving interaction history. Our subset contains 152 tasks across 17 categories; native category-specific checks determine correctness, and the aggregate is weighted by the number of tasks. This weighting reflects the composition of the evaluated subset, with categories containing more tasks contributing proportionally more to the reported aggregate. ACEBench evaluates API use under Normal, Special, and Agent settings, including ordinary function calls, incomplete or ambiguous instructions, and multi-step interactions (Chen et al., 2025). Together, these settings examine how agents translate user requests into API actions under different instruction and interaction conditions. We use 50 English tasks, which produce 57 native scoring records. We report the native weighted score and separately retain complete-task success; these quantities use different denominators. The distinction matters because one task can contribute more than one native scoring record. Record-level scoring describes the evaluators individual scoring units, whereas complete-task success summarizes outcomes at the original task level. We therefore specify both task and scoring-record counts when describing this evaluation. Multi-hop question answering. HotpotQA requires combining evidence from multiple Wikipedia passages to answer bridge or comparison questions (Yang et al., 2018). We use 100 development questions with the v1 fullwiki protocol. 2WikiMultiHopQA requires composing facts about multiple entities along multi-hop reasoning chains (Ho et al., 2020); we use 100 development questions and the original v1 evaluator. These tasks test whether agents can connect dispersed evidence and resolve questions requiring relational reasoning. For both benchmarks, the agent retrieves evidence through the search interface and submits an answer. The main metric is normalized answertoken F1, with exact match (EM) retained separately. The evaluator revisions are 3635853 for HotpotQA and 13800e5 for 2WikiMultiHopQA. A.3 TrainingEvaluation Separation We separate training-time evolution from evaluation on the 744-task reporting set. For each evaluated evolution horizon n, we first complete rounds on training tasks and then evaluate the resulting system on the reporting set. Reporting tasks are excluded from Task-model fine-tuning. Reporting-set scores and item-level evaluation feedback are never used for workflow selection, candidate acceptance, skill maintenance, Meta-Harness revision, or manual selection of system versions. 13 Table 5: Benchmarks and reporting metrics. ACEBench has 50 tasks and 57 native scoring records. QA exact match is retained separately. Benchmark Tasks Metric HumanEval+ MBPP+ BFCL-v3 ACEBench HotpotQA 2WikiMultiHopQA 164 System pass@1 178 System pass@1 152 Weighted accuracy 50 Native weighted score 100 Answer F1 100 Answer F1 Total 744 Evaluations at different horizons measure the corresponding training-derived states; their results are not fed back into subsequent evolution. The gain-based acceptance rule in the evolution algorithm applies only to training-time batches. The batch-level Artifacts procedure, including its two-attempt allowance and fallback to the parent, is not run on the reporting set. During reporting, the skill library and Meta-Harness remain fixed across tasks. Permitted environment feedback includes execution-interface signals such as context-length limit errors and output-length or format violations; it does not provide access to the reporting evaluator for optimization or output selection. Reference answers and hidden-test correctness signals are likewise excluded from generation and output selection. All compared methods receive the same environment feedback, tool permissions, and pertask execution budgets. We additionally checked the frozen training and reporting manifests for overlap in task identifiers, recorded normalized prompt hashes, and recorded task-group identifiers, finding no matches between the two sets. This check establishes separation under these matching criteria; it does not assess semantic paraphrases or contamination in the backbone models pretraining data. Equal per-task execution budgets likewise do not imply equal total evolution cost. A.4 Baseline Configurations We compare seven baselines using Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025). Within each backbone scale, the comparison protocol uses common initial checkpoint and Task-Harness, task IDs, and evaluators. Table 6 summarizes editable Task components, weight training, Harness updates, adaptive component selection, and Meta-Agent evolution. These dimensions distinguish how each baseline allocates adaptation across model parameters, task components, and orchestration. Model updates. SFT trains on successful TaskAgent trajectories while keeping the Harness fixed. GRPO samples groups of trajectories, scores their task outcomes, and updates the model using grouprelative rewards (Shao et al., 2024). Both methods improve the Task model without componentselection mechanism. Harness and joint updates. AFlow searches executable agent workflows through iterative proposal and evaluation (Zhang et al., 2025). MermaidFlow represents workflows as graphs and searches their structure (Zheng et al., 2025). These are the Harness-only configurations used in the main comparison. HarnessForge combines feedbackguided Harness modification with model training in prescribed co-adaptation procedure (Chen et al., 2026b). SIA uses execution feedback to choose between Harness and model updates (Hebbar et al., 2026). Meta-Agent evolution. HyperAgents makes both the Task-Agent and Meta-Agent programs editable, allowing the improvement procedure itself to evolve (Zhang et al., 2026c). Its code-editing mechanism differs from parameter training. RSIFlow selects among Model, Harness, and Artifacts interventions and updates its Meta-Harness through accumulated intervention skills. The comparison therefore separates access to multiple Task-update routes from the ability to revise the Meta-Agent that chooses and implements them. A.5 Hyperparameter Settings The main configuration uses Qwen3-4B or Qwen38B as the Task model and GPT-5.6 Sol as the Meta model. Each of the five evolution rounds permits at most two candidate attempts. Candidates share the same parent, training batch, and evaluator; the first valid candidate with positive paired gain is accepted. Meta model parameters remain fixed throughout evolution. Table 8 lists the supplied 4B SFT/GRPO training settings. The separate comparison uses B1 for training and B2 for evaluation, as defined in Appendix C.1; its evaluation temperature does not specify decoding for all main experiments. sections.title: E Extended Related Work
sections.content: Agent System Design and Adaptation. Recent work on LLM agents explores approaches to adapting execution structures, maintaining persistent memory, and coordinating information acquisition. HarnessForge (Chen et al., 2026b) jointly evolves execution harnesses and reasoning policies through failure-guided harness modification and harnessconditioned policy alignment. For persistent memory, All-Mem (Lv et al., 2026a) separates online retrieval from offline topology consolidation, preserving evidence while supporting retrieval under bounded computational budgets. Typed links enable budgeted expansion from anchors to archived evidence. For breadth-oriented information gathering, moreover, A-MapReduce (Chen et al., 2026c) decomposes wide-search objectives into parallel retrieval tasks and aggregates results, using experiential memory to refine task allocation and recomposition. These approaches improve how agents organize execution and retain or acquire information, with emphases on system compatibility, memory maintenance, and scalability. Structured Supervision and Credit Assignment. complementary line of research studies the structure and granularity of supervision for agent learning and language model post-training. GEAR (Lv et al., 2026b) models prerequisite and activation dependencies among rubric criteria with probabilistic graphical framework, suppressing unsupported criterion contributions when constructing scalar rewards. The resulting reward captures criterion dependencies at the response level. For long-horizon agent distillation, AlignOPSD (Chen et al., 2026a) aligns privileged supervision with functionally corresponding decisions and distributes outcomebased credit across variable-duration decision spans and their constituent turns. TRCA (Zhang et al., 2026a) derives step-level supervision from action-induced state transitions using Evidence, Execution, and Invalidity rubrics. Its foundational reward evaluates local transition quality, while its breakthrough reward recognizes newly satisfied task conditions, providing fine-grained learning signals without requiring successful reference trajectories or learned process evaluators, even when terminal success feedback is sparse.
